title: Can England's Schools Deliver Reform Without Being Overwhelmed?
label: 15 September 2026 · Schools reform, inclusion and accountability
summary: The Education Committee examined the Government's plans to reform schools in England, covering special educational needs, school trusts, vocational education, attendance, behaviour, funding and opportunities beyond classroom lessons. Across two panels, witnesses broadly welcomed the ambition to make education more inclusive and give disadvantaged children better opportunities, but warned that schools were being asked to deliver too many changes without sufficient funding or support. There were disagreements about whether academy trusts improve schools, how much control local authorities should have, and whether strict behaviour rules and performance targets help children succeed. A recurring argument was that schools should be judged not simply by examination results, but by how well they support every child, including those who struggle to attend or achieve. Witnesses called for stronger local partnerships, meaningful parental and pupil involvement, better support for teachers and clearer priorities from Government. The central message was that reform could improve education, but only if schools have the resources, flexibility and time to make it work.

Organisations responsible for running one or more state-funded schools independently of local council control.

chapters.title: Too Many Reforms, Too Little Capacity?
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses supported improving education and technical qualifications but warned that schools need funding, flexibility and realistic expectations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Schools are facing curriculum changes, new inspections and expectations to improve children's opportunities and sense of belonging. How can the Government make all this manageable?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: The White Paper contains 102 separate policy commitments. That's an enormous amount for schools to take on. We need a clear plan for what happens first, what comes later and how everything will be funded. But there's also a risk in doing nothing. Reforming SEND support is one of the most important education challenges of our generation.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Councils can help schools provide activities through libraries, leisure services and other local facilities. But schools and councils understand their own communities, so they need flexibility over how and when changes happen. Small rural schools face particular difficulties. Larger schools belonging to trusts often have more staff and resources to manage change.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: The Government has also announced new technical education options for young people. Can schools deliver them, and will they actually help pupils find jobs?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Schools may need to rethink how they teach, but it's achievable. The bigger problem is what happens afterwards. There's little point giving young people new qualifications if employers can't offer them jobs. Economic stagnation and higher employment costs are making that harder. Education reform needs to work alongside efforts to create opportunities for young people.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: There is a real problem with technical awards at age 16. Unlike GCSEs, they don't have the same nationally agreed content, standards or regulation. We think the Government should bring forward its review of these qualifications and start improving them now. They also need to connect properly with technical qualifications available after 16, so young people can continue developing their skills.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: What about rural areas like South Devon? We have fewer colleges, fewer large employers and fewer opportunities for work placements. Won't these proposals be much harder to deliver there?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Yes. Lincolnshire faces similar difficulties. Schools and councils will need to build stronger relationships with employers, but the obstacles are greater in rural communities. The Government needs to recognise that.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: We must also avoid deciding children's futures too early. If pupils are put on a particular route at 14, especially somewhere with limited local opportunities, they could become trapped in it. Education should remain broad until at least 16. Young people should be able to combine academic and technical qualifications or switch between them, rather than being locked into one route.

chapters.title: School Trusts and Accountability to Families
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses disagreed about how well academy trusts serve parents and communities, despite broad support for greater local cooperation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Government also wants more education decisions made locally. How would that work for councils and for large academy trusts, which currently answer mainly to central Government?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Giving local areas more responsibility could help tackle the number of young people outside education and employment. But what happens in areas without mayors or the same local government arrangements? Will they miss out on funding? We need councils, employers and education providers working together to support children from their earliest years right through to employment.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Trusts should see themselves as part of the communities they serve. Even large national trusts generally have local arrangements. We welcome opportunities for schools, councils and other organisations to work together on problems affecting children in their area.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Government wants every child to have two weeks of work experience. Is that realistic?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: It's a worthwhile ambition, but it needs more money and stronger links with employers. Finding enough suitable placements is particularly difficult in rural areas. We need answers about the funding and practical arrangements before we can be confident it will work.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: The Government wants schools to join or form trusts, but the evidence that trusts improve education is mixed. There are also concerns about teachers leaving academy schools. What makes you confident this is the right approach?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Our latest research finds substantial and lasting improvements in schools that joined trusts, particularly previously struggling schools in disadvantaged areas. But we can't yet prove that joining a trust caused those improvements, and results vary between trusts. Teacher retention is also disputed because official figures don't always distinguish teachers leaving the profession from those moving between schools within the same trust.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: There are also concerns about openness. Parents often struggle to find out who makes decisions in academy trusts or how to challenge them. Schools run by councils have more visible local arrangements. How do you respond?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Trusts face extensive financial checks. They must publish annual accounts, undergo independent audits and disclose their governance arrangements. In some respects, their financial oversight is stricter than that of council-run schools. But I accept that large trusts can seem distant. Having local people involved in governing individual schools is important.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: Parents in my constituency tell me that once they've spoken to the headteacher, they often don't know where else to go. And trusts operating in the same area don't always cooperate with each other. There's a real gap between the idea of community involvement and what families experience.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I'd caution against describing that as a misunderstanding. Parents aren't interested in complicated organisational structures for their own sake. They need someone to help when something goes wrong. Many MPs hear the same complaints about families struggling to get answers from trusts.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: I wasn't blaming parents. I meant there can be misunderstandings about the governance arrangements. But the rise in parental complaints is a serious issue across all types of schools, not just academies. We need to understand why families feel disconnected and improve their involvement.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: I hear similar complaints from parents, particularly when their children move to secondary school. Some trusts clearly need to improve how they communicate, although council-run schools aren't perfect either. One possibility would be for Ofsted to inspect entire trusts, rather than just individual schools, making their decisions and responsibilities clearer to families.

chapters.title: Who Decides Where Children Go to School?
chapters.takeaway: Councils need enough authority to secure school places and protect vulnerable schools, especially when individual trusts' interests conflict with local needs.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: The White Paper would allow councils to form academy trusts of their own. Would they want to do that?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Some might, but it shouldn't be compulsory. Rural councils have many small schools that existing trusts haven't taken on because they're financially difficult to run. About 90% of maintained schools are rated good or outstanding by Ofsted, so there isn't an obvious reason to force them all to change. Councils could also face financial risks or conflicts between their different responsibilities.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To clarify, the Government isn't proposing to force councils to establish trusts. It's offering them the option. Another concern is how schools and councils support families facing problems such as homelessness and transport difficulties.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: That's important, and home-to-school transport is a major gap in the White Paper. Transport for children with SEND is already putting enormous financial pressure on councils. Rural areas face different difficulties from cities, but both have problems. Even if SEND reform reduces some costs eventually, we need to know what happens in the meantime.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: What should change when schools decide which children to admit, particularly those needing a place during the school year?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: The guiding principle should be getting children into school quickly. Recent legislation gives the admissions adjudicator stronger powers, but we're still waiting for detailed rules. Schools and councils should work together so children aren't left without education for long periods.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Councils sometimes struggle when schools refuse additional pupils because they say they're full. We already have funding to help schools genuinely short of space. But when a school could accept a child and won't, councils need stronger powers to secure that place. The rules should also consider children joining later years, not just those entering at the start of secondary school.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: We're also seeing fewer children entering schools because birth rates have fallen. How should the system respond?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: In Lincolnshire, we're monitoring schools with as few as 21 pupils. Closing them should be the last option because they're central to their communities. Schools can share leadership and resources, or use spare buildings for early years education, special educational needs support or alternative education for children struggling in mainstream schools. We need a national approach to keeping small schools viable.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But cooperation isn't guaranteed. In my area, some schools have joined trusts to escape local plans to reduce unnecessary school places. Councils can't make the same decisions about academies as they can about their own schools. Sometimes a school also leaves its debts with the council when it becomes an academy. Isn't that evidence that the current arrangements fail?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: I agree. Councils need powers to ensure schools provide the places local children need, whether they're academies or maintained schools. Otherwise individual organisations can make decisions that don't work for the wider community.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: The new powers to challenge admission numbers offer one way of dealing with disputes. But I'd prefer schools and councils to reach agreements together and use formal intervention only as a last resort.

turns.speaker: Jodie Gosling
turns.text: You previously criticised RISE, the Government's programme for supporting struggling schools. Has anything improved?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Yes. Initially, schools were sometimes matched with organisations that weren't the best fit to help them improve. That caused considerable concern. The Department has since made those decisions more carefully, and the programme is working much better. We're still discussing remaining problems, but there has been substantial progress.

chapters.title: A Broader Education — But Who Pays?
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses wanted children to enjoy a wider range of activities, but opposed making schools deliver more without funding or consideration of local circumstances.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: The Government wants every child to have opportunities beyond academic lessons, including sport, arts and other activities. How can we make sure disadvantaged children and those in rural areas benefit too?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Councils can help through libraries, leisure facilities and holiday activities. The extension of the HAF programme is very welcome. In Lincolnshire, we've seen how these activities give disadvantaged children experiences they might otherwise miss. They can support children's confidence, mental health and attendance, particularly after the summer holidays. But we're still reaching only a fraction of the children who could benefit.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: These experiences are fundamental to education, not an optional luxury. They help children find what they're good at and feel that school is somewhere they belong. My concern is that funding pressures and all the other reforms could make schools less able to offer them.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: What about extending the school day? The timetable is already crowded, and schools struggle to find room for art, music, drama and sport. Could a longer day help?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Sometimes. One trust in Bedfordshire extended its day because many parents work late. Children can complete homework at school and spend more time with their families afterwards. But that's a response to local circumstances. I wouldn't make longer school days compulsory nationwide.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: There are consequences for school transport and childcare providers too. The Local Government Association doesn't currently have an official position on extending the school day.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should the Government be clearer about which activities schools must provide during lessons, before or after school, and which should come from the wider community?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: I don't think central Government should decide those details. Local schools and organisations should agree what works for their children. What would help most is more money. We also need to recognise that special schools face additional challenges, particularly when children depend on organised transport to get home.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Community groups and youth services can contribute, but access matters. A youth centre might be easy to reach in a city and practically inaccessible in a rural area without transport. Local conditions and the needs of smaller schools have to be considered.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: The Government is considering changes to Progress 8, which measures school performance across different GCSE subjects. Would you change it to encourage a broader education?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: I'd keep Progress 8. English, maths and science must remain central, but pupils also need opportunities to study other subjects. The difficulty is that adding weight to one subject means reducing the weight given to another. The current measure works reasonably well, although no measure is perfect. I want to see the Government's actual proposals before deciding whether they're improvements.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: The White Paper also proposes changing the national funding formula to better support disadvantaged pupils. Should schools have more freedom over how that money is used?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Money must continue going towards disadvantaged children. I'm not suggesting otherwise. But schools need flexibility to spend it on the support their pupils actually need, including helping teachers meet SEND needs. I should clarify that these are my comments rather than a formal Local Government Association position on the funding formula. We'll write to the Committee with that position.

chapters.title: Why Children Stop Attending School
chapters.takeaway: Attendance problems cannot be solved by targets and fines alone; witnesses stressed understanding children's circumstances and rebuilding trust between schools and families.

turns.speaker: Mrs Brackenridge
turns.text: The White Paper aims to improve attendance, behaviour and children's sense of belonging. How much responsibility should schools carry, and where do councils and other services need to help?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: It's everyone's responsibility. Councils need to support schools regardless of how they're run. Holiday activities can help children maintain routines, and better SEND support should make parents more confident that schools can meet their children's needs. I hope that will improve attendance. Inspections and stronger council powers could also help make sure schools take inclusion seriously.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Poor attendance is a wider social problem, not simply a school problem. One thing England has done well is collect daily attendance information, which helps schools see exactly when and where children are missing lessons. We should use that information to understand the problem more precisely.

turns.speaker: Mrs Brackenridge
turns.text: Should schools fine parents when children don't attend?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: We don't have an official position on fines, and there's disagreement about how effective they are. But everyone would agree they should be a last resort. We should first understand why the child isn't attending.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: There's a big difference between parents taking children on holiday because it's cheaper during term time and a family facing serious problems at home. Fining the second family could make everything worse. We need to look at individual circumstances.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I'd like to bring in our second panel. Ian, your research focuses on whether children feel they belong at school. Why does that matter?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Research consistently shows that children who feel they belong are more likely to be happy, succeed academically and have their needs met. Belonging isn't an extra programme schools should bolt on. It should shape daily life: children feeling welcome, adults understanding their needs, and families being treated as partners. If we get it right, schools can become safer places for children and staff.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What does a school actually do to create that feeling?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Relationships are central. England suspends and excludes proportionally more pupils than other parts of the UK. In Scotland, school guidance puts much more emphasis on relationships, while England tends to focus on behaviour. If we begin by treating a child's behaviour as the problem, we can miss the reasons behind it. Children need supportive relationships with staff and each other, especially during difficult transitions between schools.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: A good school has clear expectations, but it also listens to children and helps them understand why learning matters. I worry about celebrating schools simply because they're exceptionally strict. Through my work on oracy, I've seen how teaching children to speak, listen and disagree respectfully gives them confidence and a genuine role in their own education.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Children themselves must help shape what school engagement looks like. Otherwise it risks becoming another performance target used to punish schools. Pupils need a meaningful say in decisions that affect them.

turns.speaker: Mrs Brackenridge
turns.text: Around one in five young people is still persistently absent. Will setting attendance targets for individual schools solve that?

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: Something changed during covid. For some families, staying home became more normal, and the expectations between parents and schools shifted. We need to rebuild that relationship and remind parents why attendance matters, while giving them proper ways to raise concerns. Schools that are succeeding in difficult circumstances should be recognised, so others can learn from them.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: I'm worried about blaming parents. Some children avoid school because they're frightened, feel excluded or have health problems. Some parents don't even know their child is missing lessons. Others feel powerless to help. Fines often hurt families who can least afford them. Making schools welcoming and understanding why children stay away is more important.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Targets can have unintended consequences. A school might work extremely hard to improve attendance but still be judged poorly because its pupils have complicated behavioural or additional needs. We shouldn't overlook that progress or treat every school's circumstances as identical.

chapters.title: Behaviour, Teaching and Student Voice
chapters.takeaway: The second panel argued that good behaviour depends on supportive relationships, appropriate expectations and teacher training, not simply stricter rules.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: I surveyed more than 900 teachers, and around half said they were considering leaving because of pupil behaviour. How can schools maintain high standards while meeting children's different needs?

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: Managing a class has always been demanding, but adults need to demonstrate the behaviour they expect. At my school, staff spoke with children, ate alongside them and showed what respectful conversations look like. Lessons also matter. If pupils are interested, understand what they're learning and feel listened to, they're more likely to behave well.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: We need to think carefully about what we call bad behaviour. Sometimes a child isn't listening because the lesson doesn't engage them. Others are dealing with trauma, anxiety or emotional difficulties. We can't expect every child to behave identically. Teachers need training and support to respond differently where appropriate, while keeping classrooms safe and making sure everyone can learn.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: Do teachers get enough training to recognise when a child's behaviour reflects early-life trauma?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Not enough. Initial teacher training touches on these issues, but there's considerable pressure to follow a standard programme. We should spend more time teaching staff to recognise individual needs and work with others to support those children. That would help create calmer classrooms for everyone.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Some schools have gone too far with rigid rules, such as enforcing silence in corridors or extremely strict uniform policies. Those rules can create conflicts that might otherwise never happen. They don't necessarily help children feel involved or respected.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: The Government wants schools to become more connected to their communities. Should it go further?

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Yes. Schools face problems that differ enormously between communities, and national rules don't always recognise that. Local school governors are an important way for communities to influence decisions. But in some trusts, local governors have so little real power that volunteers no longer want to serve. If we want community involvement, local people need meaningful responsibility.

chapters.title: Exam Results Versus a Useful Education
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses questioned whether international rankings and conventional examinations tell the full story, and called for respected technical qualifications and greater attention to struggling pupils.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: What should we learn from the recently published PISA 2025 results, which compare pupils internationally? Do they support the Government's reforms?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: I wouldn't place too much weight on PISA. It's an imperfect measure, and some children are specifically prepared for these tests. Reading, maths and science matter, but so do relationships and whether pupils feel safe. I've seen schools where children regularly discuss their feelings and ideas together, and those schools also achieve strong academic results. Performance tables can encourage schools to chase scores rather than do what's best for pupils.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: People have used the PISA results to support very different political arguments. International comparisons ignore cultural differences, such as children in Shanghai attending extra lessons at weekends. I'd focus instead on the roughly one-third of pupils who receive grades 1, 2 or 3 in GCSE English, below the standard pass of grade 4. We keep telling them they've failed, rather than recognising what they can do. The reforms haven't properly addressed that.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: The results have already become part of political arguments. They also tell us little about the pressure on teachers and headteachers involved in achieving those outcomes. We need to consider the human cost of the system, not just its examination scores.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: How do we make sure young people develop the skills they need for employment and adult life?

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: First, we have to listen properly to children, young people and their parents. Too often, their experiences aren't central to decisions about education. There's still a lot for the Government and organisations like ours to work through.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Missing substantial amounts of school is strongly associated with later being outside education, employment or training. We need to understand that. We must also stop treating vocational qualifications as second-rate. Reviews have promised them equal status for years, but schools and employers haven't consistently valued them that way. Every subject also needs to develop literacy and communication, whether pupils are studying art, practical design, science or Shakespeare.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: The White Paper simply tries to do too much. I'd concentrate on a few things that could make a real difference: supporting children moving from primary to secondary school, fixing the GCSE problem, improving teaching and making education work for children with additional needs. When my school sent 20 pupils to a nearby college for practical courses two days a week, their English and maths results improved, alongside their behaviour and enthusiasm. Academic and practical learning can reinforce each other.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: But everyone wants to add something worthwhile, whether that's practical learning, arts or communication. How do we decide what to leave out?

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: The Government should remove some of the detailed instructions about how schools are managed and trust headteachers to set sensible goals. A good curriculum matters, but what makes the greatest difference is how well teachers bring it to life. We need to help teachers improve, give pupils a genuine sense of achievement and focus resources on children the system currently fails.

chapters.title: Making the System Work for Every Child
chapters.takeaway: The final discussion called for genuine cooperation between schools, fairer support for disadvantaged children and greater trust in local leaders.

turns.speaker: Jodie Gosling
turns.text: The Government wants all schools eventually to belong to trusts, including trusts that councils could establish. Is that the right direction?

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Before asking every school to join a trust, we need to ask what benefit that trust will provide. Some schools can't find a suitable trust, while others have joined one and regretted it. We shouldn't assume changing a school's organisational structure automatically improves education. We need convincing evidence that the move will help.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: I've seen good and bad examples on both sides. Some trusts make it easier for schools to share specialist staff, such as educational psychologists. Others make it harder for certain children to remain in their schools. Some councils provide excellent support, while others have lost so many resources that they struggle. The question shouldn't be whether trusts are inherently good or bad, but how schools get the support they need.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: The current system can reward schools for avoiding children who need extra help. I remember a parent being told by one school that their anxious child would be better off somewhere else. That's unacceptable. Schools should share responsibility for every child in their area, including those in special schools or alternative education. We need to judge the system on whether all those children are being served, not whether one school protects its own results.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What happens when a school wants to leave a distant trust and join one nearby, but its existing trust refuses to release it? I've seen exactly that happen. Shouldn't the rules make it easier for schools to join organisations that fit their local community?

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Personally, I think so, although that's not yet the official position of the National Governance Association. Some trusts expanded because they wanted more schools, rather than because those schools were a good local fit. Competition encouraged that. Some trusts now recognise that particular schools would be better elsewhere, but changing arrangements can be difficult. We need a more cooperative approach.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: Reducing the gap between disadvantaged children and their classmates is a major Government goal. What matters most: identifying disadvantage, directing resources or tackling wider problems?

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: We need to encourage excellent teachers and leaders to work in the communities facing the greatest difficulties. At present, taking a job in a struggling school can feel like a personal risk. One poor Ofsted inspection can damage a headteacher's career, even if improving the school will take years. Leaders need support and confidence that they'll be given time to make lasting changes.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Poverty exists in cities and rural communities, and children need help as early as possible. That may mean extra school funding. But I've also seen schools thrive in difficult areas because staff feel connected to the community and proud to work there. We need to learn from those examples and make sure resources reach children when they actually need them.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: We should reconsider how we define disadvantage, rather than relying on a narrow set of measures. Schools should also feel able to take chances on children with additional needs without worrying that their results will suffer. The way we judge schools currently discourages some of those decisions.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: Before Ministers take these reforms forward, what do they most need to hear from the education sector?

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Listen to local communities, especially school governors and volunteers. If schools are meant to serve their communities, those people must have a real say.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Schools need to know they won't be punished for trying to build better relationships and a more welcoming culture. That sort of change can take three years. They need support during that time, not unrealistic demands for immediate results. Schools, councils and trusts should also share expertise and scarce resources, including specialist educational psychologists.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: Give headteachers and teachers the freedom to concentrate on what will genuinely improve children's lives. The Government has set out more than a hundred additional demands, and schools simply can't do everything. Local leaders should choose the priorities that make the greatest difference, particularly for disadvantaged children, and be held accountable for the results. Trust them to make those decisions.
